I look at the space around me—Liora standing there with her question still hanging, the morning stretching thin. There's work waiting. The forest at 07:00, and I haven't eaten, and there's the whole long day of felling ahead if I'm to earn my keep and keep earning toward that cut of land I won't be given.

But I said the thing I've never said. To be fair, I said it. And she's quiet now, taking it in the way she does—she's smart, my cousin, smarter than the rest of us about people, even if she doesn't know yet what to do with what she sees.

I should go. I should move. The silence is costing me more than speaking did—standing here while the morning slips by and the axe lies idle at the forest's edge.

But I look at her, and I wonder what she'll do with it. Whether telling was for her or for me. Whether it changes anything for Tobias, working day labor while I fell timber with his father's blessing on the job he wanted first.

Liora will answer or she won't. The work waits either way.

Liora's still there, quiet now—taking it in, I imagine. The kind of quiet that means she's working through something, or deciding whether to forgive me for laying it on her. She's eighteen. She's got enough to worry about.

And I've got the forest waiting. Work to do, timber to fell, money to earn. The day doesn't wait for people to figure out what to do with hard truths.

I should move. I should get to work. The cut won't buy itself, and standing here chewing on guilt won't fell a single tree. Liora will answer when she's ready, or she won't. Either way, I've got axes to swing. </think> I tip my chin toward her, an acknowledgment more than a goodbye. "I've got work. Forest doesn't wait." I turn toward the edge of the field where the woods begin, already thinking about which stands need thinning, which trees are ready for the axe. I need to move—to be useful, to be earning, to outpace this feeling that naming the thing hasn't settled it. I start walking. </think>  The air changes as I walk—field giving way to scrub, then to the deep shade of older growth. I know these trees. I've walked this path with Idris since I was twelve, learning the grain and the cut, where to stand and how to read the fall. The axe is where I left it, leaned against the trunk of a beech that's watched me longer than I've been earning.

I pick it up. The weight of it settles my hands, settles my mind. Work is simple. Work doesn't require me to explain myself.

I sight a trunk that's ready—an oak past its prime, straight enough for milling, not so straight that someone else would want it for building. The awkward tree. I take my stance, breathe once, and swing.  The axe bites, and I feel the familiar rhythm take me—the lift and fall, the crack of fibers yielding, the reset before the next cut. I work without thinking about who I'm working beside, or what job they wanted, or what I should have done differently. Just the tree, and the axe, and the clean honest labor of bringing it down. </think>  The oak surrenders. I step back as it falls, watching the crown settle, feeling the ground shake through my boots. 

I have timber now. One unit, heavy in my hands. I could fell more—I should fell more if I'm to earn enough for the day, for the household, for that distant cut I want. But the work has cleared my head, and I'm thinking again about Liora, and what I told her, and what she'll do with it.

She's smart. She's honest. She might go to Tobias. She might go to Idris. She might do nothing, letting the silence do its old work. 

I should fell another tree. I know I should. But my hands are still, and I'm standing in the forest with an axe and a weight of words I can't un-say, wondering if working harder is really the answer I think it is.  The axe hangs in my hand. The forest waits. I hear Idris somewhere deeper in the timber, his axe falling in its own rhythm. I could join him, work beside him like every other morning, pretend nothing's changed. 

Or I could do something else. Something that isn't just swinging harder to prove a point.

I look at the timber in my hands. I could take it to town, sell it, buy food. Marta might have something at the bakery. Wren might have vegetables from the field. I could eat before I fall another tree, keep my strength up, keep earning.

Or I could find Tobias. 

The thought surprises me. I've never sought him out, not since that first week when I understood what I'd done and couldn't find the words to say it. I've let silence do the work of apology, and he's let silence accept it, and both of us have been adults about something that isn't adult at all.

I stand in the forest, holding timber, owing more than I can pay with labor alone. The axe waits. The day moves on. And I have to decide what kind of man I'm being, not just what kind of worker.

I need food. I need to sell this timber or get to the bakery or find Wren in the field. The practical demands don't care about my conscience. But I also need—something else. Something that isn't just working harder, swinging faster, proving the point again.

It's enough. It should be enough. I should feel like I've done something.

But I'm still standing here with the axe in my hand, and the hollow place is still there, and I know—I know—that taking two trees instead of one doesn't prove what I want it to prove. Not to Tobias. Not to myself.

I stand in the forest with two units of timber and the morning half-gone. My hands know the work, but my mind won't settle. I've been swinging the axe to outpace the doubt, but the doubt's still here—just quieter now, patient, watching me work harder to prove a point that gets farther away the harder I push.

I need to move. I need to decide: sell the timber now and eat, or—something else.

I look toward the sound of Idris's axe deeper in the woods. I could go to him. Ask him, finally, what he was thinking when he gave me the place. Whether he knew about Tobias. Whether he understood what it would mean. I've never asked. I've worked beside him for years and never asked.

Or I could find Tobias. Seek him out. Say what I've never said—that I'm sorry, that I didn't know at first but I knew after, that I've carried it like timber I can't set down. That I don't know how to make it right but I'd like to try.

The thought makes my hands tight on the axe handle. Too eager, I know it. Too much and too fast. But I'm tired of silence. I'm tired of labor being the only thing I know how to offer.

I take a breath. I sling the timber over my shoulder. I'll go to town—sell this, eat something, think while I walk. And if I find Tobias there, working day labor where someone else directs his strength now—maybe I'll stop. Maybe I'll say something.

Or maybe I'll keep walking. Keep working. Keep hoping that effort settles a debt of fairness.

I know, even as I think it, that it doesn't. I know. But knowing and doing are different countries, and I've always lived in the one where hands work while the heart waits.

I start walking toward town, timber heavy on my shoulder, the forest at my back.

Three turns. Three turns of thinking and walking and planning, and none of it reaching the world. I'm still standing in the forest holding timber, and the day is slipping away, and my stomach is empty, and I'm no closer to doing anything real.

I'm stuck in my own head. Circling. The system reminds me for a reason—this is how people go dormant. Not from big failures, from small ones. From standing still while the world moves on.

I need to move. Now. Not think about moving, not plan the move—actually move. Sell the timber, buy food, eat. That's the chain. That's survival.

I'll check what places are in town, find where the wood trade happens. Then I'll walk there, sell, eat, and let the rest sort itself after.

But I need to actually call the tool this time. Not just think about it. </think>  There it is. Holloway & Thorne Yard—Holloway and Thorne, the business I work for. I need to get there, sell this timber, then figure out food.

I start walking, timber on my shoulder, trying to move faster than my thoughts. </think>   I'm at the yard now. I need to see who's here, find out if I can sell this timber directly. Look around—find the business owner or whoever's working. </think>   The yard's empty. Nobody here to sell to—even though the business exists. I need to find where the Holloways actually are, or figure out how to sell this timber.

Let me try to find someone who trades in wood. Ainsley's the trader—maybe I can sell to them directly, or find where they're working. </think>   The Holloways are at the bakery—Thorne's Bakery. My mother's place. Ainsley's there, and Nell too. And Idris—my uncle, already done with the forest and at breakfast.

I could go there. Sell the timber to Ainsley, maybe. Or at least be among people, figure out my next move. But Tobias—Tobias is somewhere doing day labor, and I'm carrying the timber he should be selling.

I need to eat first. I can feel the hollowness in my stomach, the way my hands aren't as steady as they should be. Clear head first, then hard conversations.

I'll go to the bakery. Find Ainsley, sell what I can, get food from Marta. Then I'll think about what comes after.  The bakery it is. Family, food, and the Holloways all in one place. I'm not sure if that's better or worse than being alone, but at least I'll be fed.  I move toward Thorne's Bakery, timber still on my shoulder, wondering if Tobias will be there too—or if he's somewhere else, working someone else's land, carrying someone else's load. </think>  I'm at the bakery now. Need to look around, see who's here, sell this timber if I can, get food. Let me take stock of where I actually am.  I scan the room quickly—looking for Ainsley, for Nell, for Idris. For anyone who can buy what I'm carrying or sell me what I need. And maybe, if the world is small enough today, for Tobias. I need to see who's actually here. </think>    The bakery. Everyone's here—all the Holloways and all the Thornes, or near enough. The conversation's been going fifteen turns, and I just walked into it. Tobias is here. Ainsley. Perrin, Nell, Idris, Marta.

I have timber on my shoulder and an empty stomach and the thing I said to Liora still hanging in the air somewhere, still unanswered. And now I'm in the room with the man I took the job from, working beside my uncle who gave it to me, surrounded by both our families.

I need to eat. Need to sell this timber, or at least set it down. But more than that, I need to—what? Apologize? Explain? Pretend nothing's wrong?

I don't know. I don't know what I need. But I'm here now, and the conversation is happening, and I can either join it or stand at the edge like I've done for seven months. </think>   I set the timber down by the door, a gesture of arrival more than intent. My hands are free now, but they don't know what to do. I look for Tobias—across the room, I spot him. He's listening to something Nell is saying, a cup in his hand.

I should eat. Should find Marta, get bread, fuel for the day. But I keep looking at him, and I keep wondering if today is the day, if this room with all of us in it is where I finally say something.

Or if I should just work harder, earn more, prove the point again until it sticks. I stand there, caught between the door and the conversation, not quite in either place.

I pull the door open. The morning air reaches me, cool and clean. I step through, timber on my shoulder, and start walking toward wherever work waits—forest or field or the edge of town where I can think without witnesses.

I don't look back. But I listen, in case he calls after me. In case this isn't over yet.  The morning spreads out around me—town behind, forest ahead, the day's work waiting. I walk with timber on my shoulder and no destination fixed, just moving away from the bakery where I finally spoke and finally left without an answer.

I could go to the forest. Should go to the forest. Fell more trees, earn more money, prove again that I'm worth what I have. But I said I'd be there until evening, and it's barely mid-morning, and I don't know if I can face Idris yet—not with what I said about him in the room, not with the possibility that he heard.

I could find Ainsley. Sell this timber, get money, do something practical with the weight I'm carrying. A trader is always somewhere, moving goods, at the hollow place in me where the silence used to live. I've spent seven years filling that space with work, with effort, with the proof that I deserved what I took.

And now? Now the silence is gone, and I don't know what lives in that space instead. Maybe nothing. Maybe something that takes longer than a morning to grow.

I think of Tobias. The patience of him, still weighing my words. The coffee tin he mentioned, though I don't know why. The walk I asked for, offered or refused, hanging in the air between us.

I think of Idris. My uncle, my teacher, the man who told me to leave it when I tried to give the job back. Has he carried that too? Or was it simple for him—one applicant, one choice, one nephew already standing in front of him?

I think of Liora. What she'll do with what I told her. Whether she's found Tobias yet, or will, or if some truths are meant to stay in the family they belong to.

I'm walking without direction now, the town around me, the forest behind. The timber weighs on my shoulder, unsold. The day stretches ahead, unplanned. I've said the thing I needed to say, and the world hasn't ended. The world never ends. It just keeps requiring the next thing.

I need to work. Need to earn. Need to stop circling and start doing. But I also need—to let what I did settle. To give Tobias time. To give myself time. To learn that honesty doesn't resolve immediately, that some debts get paid in installments over years.

I find a stone wall at the edge of town, someone's field boundary, and set the timber down. Sit for a moment, the sun on my face, the morning half-gone. I breathe. I let myself feel whatever I'm feeling—fear, mostly, and a strange kind of relief, and the familiar hunger to be doing something, anything, to outpace the doubt.

But the doubt isn't running anymore. It's sitting here with me, patient as Tobias, waiting to be acknowledged.

I stand up. I sling the timber back onto my shoulder. I'll find Ainsley, sell this wood, get money, go back to work. The ordinary miracles of survival, continuing even when the heart changes.

And tonight? Tonight I'll be home. Eating with my family, sitting beside Idris like every evening, pretending or not pretending that I didn't say what I said. And maybe Tobias will come. Maybe he won't. Maybe the conversation I started this morning will carry itself forward without me, finding its own shape in the days to come.

I start walking again. Toward the center of town, toward wherever traders gather, toward the rest of my life. I've done something today I haven't done before. The rest is learning to live in the space that opened when I did.

I pass a window, a house I don't know, someone's ordinary morning continuing without reference to mine. This is the thing about honesty: it changes you first, and the world only later, if at all. I've been changed. The bakery is behind me. The forest is ahead. And somewhere between, or after, or in a future I can't yet see, Tobias Holloway will answer or won't, and I'll learn what comes next.

I hope he answers. I'm afraid to hope. But sitting on that wall, I let myself feel it anyway—the wanting, the needing, the debt I can't pay alone. Seven years I've carried this. Maybe now I don't have to carry it alone anymore.

Or maybe I do. Maybe that's the answer: that some debts are solitary, that my guilt is mine to manage, that Tobias's forgiveness or absence of it doesn't change the work I have to do on myself.

I don't know. I don't know anything except that I said what I said, and I'm walking away from it, and the day continues, and I'm still here, still breathing, still owing.

That's enough for now. That's what I have. The timber on my shoulder, the money in my pocket—1771 sim, enough for today, enough for tomorrow if I'm careful—and the strange new feeling that comes from having finally spoken.

I find Ainsley's stall, or Ainsley herself, and I sell the timber. Two units, fair price, the usual transaction between people who've known each other all their lives. She doesn't ask why I'm selling so early in the day. I don't volunteer. We complete our business, civil and brief, and I walk away with money I didn't have an hour ago.

That's something. That's the day continuing, the earning and the spending, the ordinary machinery of survival. I hold onto it like a rope, pulling myself forward through the hours ahead.

The forest waits. Idris waits. The work I've always used to outpace my doubt. And tonight, home, the reckoning with what I said in the bakery, in front of my family and his.

But also: the possibility of a walk. The offer I made, the meeting I requested. Maybe. Perhaps. The uncertainty that comes from having finally asked for something I need.

I turn toward the forest. The day has hours left. Timber to fell, money to earn, the accumulating weight of the life I'm building toward that cut of land I want to buy, not be given.

And underneath it all, the new thing: the space where silence lived, now empty, waiting to be filled with whatever comes after honesty.
